## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 1/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
State of the art (as of July 2026) in AI coding-agent governance and harness design — the problem space of the claude.md-workflow repo: project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style), lifecycle hooks, deterministic verification gates, persistent agent memory/working-state across sessions and compaction, behavioral guardrails against scope creep/overclaiming/sycophancy, git-level enforcement, task contracts, and parallel multi-agent orchestration (worktree isolation, orchestrator/reduce patterns, adversarial review). Survey and compare best practices from: Anthropic (Claude Code, Agent SDK, skills/hooks/subagents), OpenAI (Codex, AGENTS.md), Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft (GitHub Copilot agents, AutoGen/agent frameworks), NVIDIA (agent toolkits/NeMo), xAI (Grok agents/coding); and non-Western labs: Moonshot AI (Kimi K2.5 agentic training), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM-5.x coding agents), DeepSeek (agentic/tool-use practices), Tencent (recent Hunyuan model launch and agent tooling), MiniMax (M-series agentic models), Alibaba Qwen if relevant; plus respected independents: Nous Research (Hermes 4/Hermes agent), Fundamental Research Labs (Peter Wang co-founder), the team behind the Ornith-1.0 LLM, tinygrad/George Hotz's approach to minimal harnesses, and any other influential open agent-harness projects (e.g. OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin/Cognition). For each: what they prescribe for instruction-file structure and length, memory persistence, verification/eval gating, multi-agent patterns, and prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement. Identify convergent consensus, notable divergences (especially Western vs Chinese lab practices), and concrete, citable insights that should shape a 2026 rewrite of a drop-in governance kit for coding agents. Note if any named entity cannot be verified to exist (e.g. 'Ornith-1.0') rather than guessing.

## Claim under review
"A Cross-Model Critic — an agent from a different model family given minimal context — catches correlated training-data errors that same-family review misses: in the libfuse campaign it found correctness errors in 3 of 19 (~16%) fixes that same-family review had approved, and surfaced 3 additional bugs same-family review missed."

**Source:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049 (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "In the libfuse campaign specifically, CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (∼16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes and independently surfaced 3 bugs that same-family review had missed"

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

# Paper Summary

**Title:** "Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery"

**Author:** Abhinav Agarwal

**Abstract:** The paper addresses false positives in LLM-assisted security defect discovery through a multi-stage filtering system combining candidate generation, adversarial review, and cross-model evaluation. The methodology achieved approximately 79-83% rejection rates for false findings before disclosure.

---

## Key Findings from the Content

**Cross-Model Critic (CMC):** Yes, explicitly mentioned. The abstract states the approach combines "a Cross-Model Critic (CMC)" as part of its filtering mechanism.

**Libfuse Campaign:** Not mentioned in the provided content.

**Statistics on correctness errors:** Not present. The page does not include the specific statistic "3/19 (~16%) correctness errors in same-family-approved fixes."

The paper's main quantitative claim is: "on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n=30), the prospective kill rate was 83%"—referring to rejection rates, not approval accuracy metrics.

Web search results for query: ""Cross-Model Critic" libfuse "same-family" review coding agent"

Links: [{"title":"Refute-or-Promote: Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2604.19049"},{"title":"Cross-Model Code Review - Auto Learning Agents","url":"https://www.autolearningagents.com/ai-code-review/cross-model-review.php"},{"title":"(PDF) Cross-Model LLM Code Review: Should you use Claude to review Codex or vice versa?","url":"https://www.researchgate.net/publication/407032793_Cross-Model_LLM_Code_Review_Should_you_use_Claude_to_review_Codex_or_vice_versa"},{"title":"GitHub - pelednoam/multi-model-code-review-agent · GitHub","url":"https://github.com/pelednoam/multi-model-code-review-agent"},{"title":"Cross-model AI code review exposes the limits of single-model judgment","url":"https://nhimg.org/articles/cross-model-ai-code-review-exposes-the-limits-of-single-model-judgment/"},{"title":"Frontier Coding Agents Use Metaprogramming to Adapt to Unfamiliar Programming Languages","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10933"},{"title":"The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.13175"},{"title":"Adversarial Code Review | ASDLC.io","url":"https://asdlc.io/patterns/adversarial-code-review/"},{"title":"Adversarial Code Review - OpenClaw AI Agent Skill | LLMBase","url":"https://llmbase.ai/openclaw/adversarial-code-review/"}]

Based on the search results, here's what I found about "Cross-Model Critic," libfuse, and "same-family" review in the context of coding agents:

## Cross-Model Critic (CMC)

The Cross-Model Critic (CMC) is a mechanism where one or more agents from a different model family receive minimal context (a candidate summary and entry points) and perform an independent critique.

## Same-Family vs. Cross-Family Review

CMC complements same-family adversarial critique by having same-family critics catch reasoning errors a single agent missed, while the cross-family critic catches correlated training-data errors that same-family review tends to miss when replicas fail similarly.

## Application to libfuse Campaign

In the libfuse campaign, cross-family review found correctness issues in 3/19 findings that had survived earlier stages. This demonstrates how cross-model criticism can catch false positives that same-family review would miss.

## Broader Context

The research highlights a fundamental principle: when the same model family that generates code is also responsible for reviewing it, there is a risk that generative and review blind spots are correlated: the agent may fail to flag the very pattern of vulnerability that its generation tendency produces. Using independent model families for review helps mitigate this issue.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

# libfuse and Cross-Model Critic Analysis

## The 3/19 Finding

The paper states regarding libfuse:

> "Codex (a different model family) found 3 bugs that same-family review missed and identified correctness issues in 3 of 19 **proposed fixes** (16%)"

This explicitly refers to **proposed fixes**, not defect findings or candidate reports. The CMC caught correctness errors in fixes that same-family agents had already approved.

## CMC Surfacing Additional Bugs

The exact passage reads:

> "CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (∼16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes and independently surfaced 3 bugs that same-family review had missed"

This describes two distinct outcomes: (1) errors in 19 proposed fixes, and (2) 3 additional vulnerabilities that same-family review overlooked entirely.

## Context

The libfuse campaign also produced 2 CVEs and 2 merged non-CVE hardening fixes, demonstrating that cross-model verification added measurable value beyond same-family agent consensus.

The full text confirms these were proposed FIXES (not defect findings), matching the claim's framing, and names Codex (a different model family) as the cross-model critic: "Codex (a different model family) found 3 bugs that same-family review missed and identified correctness issues in 3 of 19 proposed fixes (16%)." The 'correlated training-data errors' mechanism is the paper's own stated rationale (same-family generative and review blind spots are correlated), so the claim does not overreach the source. The paper is current (April 2026) and corroborated in spirit by independent cross-model-review literature (e.g., ResearchGate "Cross-Model LLM Code Review: Should you use Claude to review Codex or vice versa?"; nhimg.org "Cross-model AI code review exposes the limits of single-model judgment"). No contradicting evidence found. Caveats that keep confidence below high: single-author arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed), one campaign, small n (19 fixes / 3 errors), no independent replication — but the claim is explicitly scoped to "the libfuse campaign," so source strength matches claim strength.
